heading: 3.2.1 Spacing class and the degree dual-role
text:
#### 3.2.1 Spacing class and the degree dual-role [LUNI.3.2.1]

The separator is optional for every unit ([LUNI.3.1.1]), so
`45°` and `45_°` are both degree, and `23°C` and `23_°C` are both
celsius.

What the degree glyph does have is a **dual role in the suffix
alphabet**: `°` is both a complete suffix on its own (degree) and the
first character of longer suffixes (`°C`, `°F`, `°R`). The lexer takes
the longest suffix available, so `45°` is degree and `45°C` is celsius —
resolved by the suffix, not by the separator.

#### Canonical name vs Unicode alias convention

The standard library uses ASCII word forms as canonical unit names (the name
valid in schema field declarations) and Unicode SI symbols as aliases (valid
in unit literals only, per §7.5). One deliberate exception: `Hz` is the
canonical name for hertz (not `hertz`), because `freq: Hz` is the universal
convention in practice and `freq: hertz` would surprise every user. Examples:

| Canonical name | Unicode alias | Schema field | Literal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `celsius` | `°C` | `temp: celsius` | `23_°C` or `23_celsius` |
| `ohm` | `Ω` | `resistance: ohm` | `100_Ω` or `100_ohm` |
| `microsecond` | `µs` | `duration: microsecond` | `500_µs` or `500_microsecond` |
| `degree` | `°` | `bearing: degree` | `45°` or `45_deg` |
| `arcsecond` | `″` | `dec: arcsecond` | `45″` or `45_arcsec` |

Authors who prefer the Unicode form in literals may use it freely. Schema
field declarations always use the ASCII canonical name.
